questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder praises one nurse as “the only person who understands me,” then calls the same nurse “awful” after a limit is set. Which pattern is the nurse observing?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sublimation, in which an unacceptable impulse is redirected into an activity that is safer or more socially acceptable to the individual.","B":"Splitting, in which the same person is viewed in sharply polarized all-good or all-bad terms rather than as having mixed qualities.","C":"Reaction formation, in which a person behaves in a way that is opposite to an unacceptable underlying feeling or impulse.","D":"Rationalization, in which a person constructs a plausible explanation to make an uncomfortable action or feeling seem more acceptable."}}
questions.rationale: The rapid shift from idealizing to devaluing the same person is consistent with splitting, a pattern of polarized perception commonly associated with borderline personality disorder. It differs from rationalization, sublimation, and reaction formation.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Borderline Personality Disorder
questions.source_detail: Clinical references describe splitting and marked shifts between idealization and devaluation as characteristic patterns in borderline personality disorder.

questions.stem: A client receives insulin glargine once daily and rapid-acting insulin with meals. A colleague suggests drawing both insulins into one syringe. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Mix the insulins if the combined dose is administered within five minutes because timing prevents a clinically meaningful change in absorption.","B":"Mix the insulins only when both are drawn from vials because the prohibition applies to prefilled pens rather than the glargine formulation.","C":"Dilute the glargine first and then combine it with rapid-acting insulin because dilution prevents precipitation and preserves its action profile.","D":"Administer insulin glargine separately because current labeling states that it must not be diluted or mixed with any other insulin or solution."}}
questions.rationale: Current insulin glargine labeling states that the product must not be diluted or mixed with any other insulin or solution. It should therefore be administered separately from rapid-acting mealtime insulin.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Insulin Glargine
questions.source_detail: DailyMed dosing instructions explicitly state: do not dilute or mix insulin glargine with any other insulin or solution.

questions.stem: A postoperative client using opioid PCA becomes too drowsy to press the demand button. The client's spouse asks whether they should press it when the client appears uncomfortable. Which response is safest?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Allow the spouse to activate demand doses whenever the client grimaces because family observation is more reliable than the client's level of alertness.","B":"Have nursing staff press the demand button at scheduled intervals because clinician activation preserves analgesia when the client is temporarily sleepy.","C":"Do not allow proxy activation; the client's inability to self-dose is a safety signal that requires assessment for sedation and respiratory depression.","D":"Increase the lockout interval and then allow family activation because a longer interval removes the additional risk created by PCA-by-proxy dosing."}}
questions.rationale: Patient-controlled analgesia relies on the patient being awake enough to activate the demand dose. Activation by family or staff can bypass this safety feature. A client who is too drowsy to self-dose requires assessment for opioid-related sedation and respiratory compromise rather than proxy dosing.
questions.source_name: AHRQ PSNet — Fatal Patient-Controlled Analgesia Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
questions.source_detail: AHRQ PSNet identifies PCA-by-proxy as a safety risk and emphasizes ongoing assessment of patients receiving PCA.

questions.stem: During administration of a vesicant antineoplastic drug through a peripheral IV, the client reports new burning and the site begins to swell. What should the nurse do first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stop the infusion immediately while leaving the catheter in place so residual drug may be aspirated and drug-specific extravasation management can begin.","B":"Increase the infusion rate to finish the vesicant quickly because reducing total contact time within the vein limits the extent of local tissue injury.","C":"Remove the catheter immediately before any aspiration is attempted because leaving the device in place can force more medication into surrounding tissue.","D":"Flush the line vigorously with normal saline to disperse the medication because dilution within the tissue is the recommended first response to extravasation."}}
questions.rationale: The 2025 ONS/ASCO extravasation guidance recommends acting immediately when extravasation is suspected: stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place initially, attempt aspiration of residual drug, and then follow agent-specific antidote and thermal-management guidance.
questions.source_name: Oncology Nursing Society — ONS/ASCO Extravasation Guideline
questions.source_detail: ONS/ASCO algorithm: stop infusion immediately, leave catheter in place initially for aspiration/management, and proceed with agent-specific interventions.

questions.stem: A client with congenital long-QT syndrome has an order for ondansetron. Which nursing action is most appropriate before administration?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Give the dose as ordered because ondansetron affects the QT interval only in clients who also have severe hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia.","B":"Clarify the order because current labeling advises avoiding ondansetron in congenital long-QT syndrome due to QT prolongation and torsades risk.","C":"Administer the medication with a beta blocker because rate control reliably eliminates the proarrhythmic effect of ondansetron in long-QT syndrome.","D":"Give the dose and obtain an ECG only if syncope occurs because routine risk assessment before ondansetron is unnecessary in congenital long-QT syndrome."}}
questions.rationale: Ondansetron labeling reports QT prolongation and postmarketing torsades de pointes and advises avoiding the drug in patients with congenital long-QT syndrome. ECG monitoring is recommended for additional risk groups such as electrolyte abnormalities, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Ondansetron
questions.source_detail: Current labeling: avoid ondansetron in congenital long-QT syndrome; QT prolongation and torsades de pointes have been reported.

questions.stem: A client taking oral ferrous sulfate for iron-deficiency anemia calls because the stools have become dark. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stop the iron immediately because dark stool during treatment indicates gastrointestinal hemorrhage until a clinician determines otherwise.","B":"Double the next iron dose because dark stool indicates inadequate absorption and shows that the prescribed dose is not reaching the bloodstream effectively.","C":"Take each dose with calcium or dairy because these foods reduce stool discoloration while improving absorption of elemental iron substantially.","D":"Explain that dark stool can occur with oral iron, while teaching the client to report tarry stool with bleeding symptoms or other concerning changes."}}
questions.rationale: Darkening of stool is a common effect of oral iron. However, black tarry stool accompanied by symptoms suggesting gastrointestinal bleeding should not automatically be attributed to iron; concerning bleeding features require clinical evaluation.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus — Taking iron supplements
questions.source_detail: Patient guidance recognizes dark stools as a common effect of iron therapy while advising medical review for concerning stool characteristics or symptoms.

questions.stem: A client with gout has started allopurinol for urate lowering and develops an acute flare during therapy. Which teaching is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stop allopurinol during every flare because continuing urate-lowering therapy prevents anti-inflammatory treatment from working effectively.","B":"Double the allopurinol dose during the flare because rapid urate reduction provides immediate analgesia and is the preferred treatment for acute pain.","C":"Continue allopurinol unless another reason to stop exists and treat the acute flare concurrently with appropriate anti-inflammatory therapy.","D":"Use allopurinol only as needed during painful flares because intermittent dosing prevents hypersensitivity and provides the strongest acute symptom relief."}}
questions.rationale: Current allopurinol labeling states that if a gout flare occurs during treatment, allopurinol need not be discontinued; the flare should be managed concurrently. Allopurinol is a long-term urate-lowering therapy, not an acute analgesic.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Allopurinol Tablets
questions.source_detail: Current labeling states that allopurinol need not be discontinued when a gout flare occurs during treatment; manage the flare concurrently.

questions.stem: A client with osteoporosis and reflux disease is prescribed weekly alendronate. Which statement shows correct understanding of administration?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"I will take it after getting up with 6 to 8 ounces of plain water, before food or other medicines, and remain upright for at least 30 minutes.","B":"I will take it with coffee and breakfast so the medication is buffered by food, then lie down for 30 minutes afterward to improve absorption.","C":"I will take it at bedtime with calcium because taking both together improves bisphosphonate binding and minimizes esophageal exposure.","D":"I will dissolve it in juice before taking it because acidic beverages improve bioavailability and reduce irritation of the upper gastrointestinal tract."}}
questions.rationale: Alendronate labeling directs patients to take the tablet after rising with 6–8 ounces of plain water, at least 30 minutes before food, drink, or other medication, and to remain upright for at least 30 minutes and until after the first food of the day.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Alendronate Sodium
questions.source_detail: Current labeling: take with 6–8 ounces plain water before food/medications and do not lie down for at least 30 minutes.

questions.stem: A client taking phenelzine plans to eat aged cheese and cured meats at a family event. Which teaching is most important?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These foods are recommended because aging lowers tyramine enough to prevent clinically important MAOI interactions during treatment.","B":"Avoid high-tyramine aged or fermented foods because their interaction with phenelzine can precipitate a dangerous hypertensive crisis.","C":"Eat the foods only with an antacid because reduced gastric acidity prevents tyramine absorption and makes the interaction clinically insignificant.","D":"Skip phenelzine on the day of the event because one missed dose reliably removes the interaction risk while allowing unrestricted food choices."}}
questions.rationale: Phenelzine labeling warns that tyramine-rich foods, including aged cheeses and dry/cured sausages, can precipitate hypertensive crises during MAOI therapy. Dietary restrictions cannot be made safe by skipping a single dose or taking an antacid.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Phenelzine Sulfate Tablets
questions.source_detail: Current labeling warns that aged, fermented, pickled, smoked, or otherwise high-tyramine foods can precipitate hypertensive crises.

questions.stem: After a procedure using midazolam, a client has persistent benzodiazepine sedation. Which statement about flumazenil is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It reverses opioids as well as benzodiazepines, so it eliminates the need to determine which sedatives or analgesics the client received.","B":"It is preferred in chronic benzodiazepine dependence because rapid receptor reversal lowers rather than increases the risk of withdrawal seizures.","C":"It can reverse benzodiazepine sedation, but seizure risk and resedation must be considered, especially with dependence or high-risk coingestants.","D":"It has no role after procedural midazolam because its approved use is limited to anticoagulant reversal and it does not affect benzodiazepine receptors."}}
questions.rationale: Flumazenil is indicated for complete or partial reversal of benzodiazepine sedation, including procedural sedation. Labeling also warns about seizures in high-risk patients and recommends monitoring for resedation and recurrent respiratory depression after reversal.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Flumazenil Injection
questions.source_detail: Current labeling supports reversal of benzodiazepine sedation and warns about seizures in high-risk patients plus resedation after reversal.

questions.stem: A client takes sublingual nitroglycerin for angina and develops a throbbing headache with mild lightheadedness. Blood pressure remains adequate. Which response is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Tell the client that the symptoms indicate nitrate allergy and that all future nitrate therapy should be avoided regardless of cardiovascular need.","B":"Encourage the client to stand and walk immediately because remaining seated increases venous pooling and worsens nitrate-related lightheadedness.","C":"Advise the client to repeat doses continuously until the headache stops because headache indicates that the previous dose was below therapeutic strength.","D":"Explain that headache and dizziness are recognized nitrate effects, keep the client safe from falls, and continue blood-pressure and symptom monitoring."}}
questions.rationale: Nitroglycerin commonly causes headache and can cause dizziness or postural hypotension because of vasodilation. In a hemodynamically stable client, these findings should be recognized and monitored rather than misclassified as allergy; safety precautions are appropriate when lightheadedness occurs.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Nitroglycerin Sublingual Tablets
questions.source_detail: Current labeling lists headache and dizziness among the most common adverse effects and warns that severe hypotension can occur.

questions.stem: An adult with suspected infection has a MAP of 58 mm Hg, mottled skin, altered mentation, and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. Septic shock is strongly suspected. Which action best reflects the current Surviving Sepsis Campaign approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait for final culture identification before starting antimicrobials so therapy can be narrowed from the first dose and unnecessary broad coverage is avoided.","B":"Begin sepsis resuscitation immediately, obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible, measure lactate, and give antimicrobials without avoidable delay.","C":"Delay antimicrobials for up to three hours because rapid diagnostic assessment should precede treatment even when the patient has clinical evidence of septic shock.","D":"Give a fixed 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus before individual assessment because the guideline treats this volume as a mandatory first step for suspected infection."}}
questions.rationale: Sepsis and septic shock are medical emergencies. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobials, lactate measurement, immediate resuscitation, and immediate antimicrobial therapy for septic shock, ideally within 1 hour. The suggested 30 mL/kg initial crystalloid volume applies to sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock in the first 3 hours and requires ongoing reassessment rather than automatic use in every suspected infection.
questions.source_name: Society of Critical Care Medicine — Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026
questions.source_detail: 2026 adult guideline: cultures ASAP ideally before antimicrobials; measure lactate; sepsis/septic shock treatment begins immediately; septic shock antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour; fluids individualized and reassessed.

questions.stem: Immediately before incision for a spinal procedure, the circulating nurse finds that the signed consent lists the left side but the operating-room schedule lists the right side. What should the team do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Proceed because the signed consent is the controlling document, and correct the operating-room schedule after the procedure is completed and documented.","B":"Ask the surgeon privately which side is intended, then proceed if the surgeon confirms the left side without repeating verification with the full procedure team.","C":"Stop progression toward incision and resolve the discrepancy through the preprocedure verification process and final team time-out before the procedure begins.","D":"Rely on the site mark alone because a visible mark replaces the need to reconcile conflicting documents during the final verification process."}}
questions.rationale: The Universal Protocol requires discrepancies to be reconciled before the procedure proceeds. The final time-out immediately before incision uses active team communication to verify the correct patient, procedure, and site; one clinician's private confirmation or a single document does not replace team verification.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Universal Protocol / Final Time-Out
questions.source_detail: Current Universal Protocol guidance requires final verification with the immediate procedure team and reconciliation of discrepancies before the procedure begins.

questions.stem: An older adult admitted with acute confusion cannot name home medications. The spouse brings medication bottles, and the community pharmacy can provide dispensing records. What is the safest admission approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Enter the medications the client can personally name and defer outside-source verification because family and pharmacy information may conflict with the client's recollection.","B":"Continue medications found in the brought-in bottles unless an admission order explicitly discontinues them, because possession suggests they remain part of the regimen.","C":"Delay medication reconciliation until discharge because admission orders should be based on the acute diagnosis rather than the outpatient medication history.","D":"Create the best possible medication list from reliable sources, compare it with current orders, and resolve and document discrepancies before the regimen is finalized."}}
questions.rationale: Medication reconciliation requires building the best possible current medication list from reliable available sources, comparing that list with admission orders, and resolving discrepancies. Relying only on the confused client's recall, blindly continuing bottles, or waiting until discharge creates avoidable omission, duplication, and interaction risk.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Effectively Managing Medications
questions.source_detail: Medication reconciliation is a transition-of-care safety process intended to maintain and communicate accurate medication information and resolve discrepancies.

questions.stem: Two hospitalized clients with the same last name are in adjacent rooms. Before administering a high-alert medication, which identification method is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use at least two person-specific identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, and match them with the medication record before administration.","B":"Use the room number and last name because the combination identifies the client reliably when the rooms and assignments were recently confirmed.","C":"Ask another nurse to visually identify the client because recognition by a staff member is an acceptable substitute for two patient identifiers.","D":"Use the client's diagnosis and bed location because clinical information is more specific than demographic identifiers during medication administration."}}
questions.rationale: The Joint Commission requires at least two person-specific identifiers when providing care, treatment, or services. A room number or physical location is not an acceptable patient identifier. Matching two identifiers to the medication record reduces wrong-patient error risk.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Patient Identification
questions.source_detail: Use at least two person-specific identifiers; room number or physical location is not an acceptable unique patient identifier.

questions.stem: After a near miss involving hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE, the medication-safety team reviews storage and labeling. Which change best addresses this risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Remind nurses to memorize the spelling difference and leave the medications together because experienced clinicians should distinguish similar names without system changes.","B":"Separate the look-alike medications, use approved name-differentiation strategies and barcode safeguards, and review storage and labeling for additional risk reduction.","C":"Remove barcode scanning for these medications because scanning can distract staff from reading labels and increases reliance on automated identification systems.","D":"Store the medications alphabetically in the same bin and add a general warning sign because consistent alphabetic placement is the strongest defense against name confusion."}}
questions.rationale: HydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE are a classic look-alike/sound-alike risk. Medication-safety design uses system defenses such as name differentiation, separation where appropriate, barcode verification, and review of packaging/storage rather than relying on memory alone.
questions.source_name: Institute for Safe Medication Practices — Confused Drug Names
questions.source_detail: ISMP maintains resources for confused drug names and recommends system-level risk-reduction strategies such as name differentiation and safer storage/verification practices.

questions.stem: On a telemetry unit, frequent nonactionable alarms have led staff to silence alarms reflexively, and a true lethal arrhythmia alarm was recently missed. Which systems response best addresses this hazard?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce alarm volume across the unit during high-noise periods and rely more heavily on visual displays so repeated alerts are less disruptive to staff workflow overall.","B":"Disable repeated alarms after the first notification because a previously acknowledged alarm no longer needs to remain audible if the condition continues.","C":"Individualize alarm limits when clinically appropriate, reduce nonactionable alarms through policy, and ensure actionable alarms remain audible and promptly addressed.","D":"Use the same default alarm limits for clients on the unit because standardization is more important than tailoring thresholds to the monitored condition."}}
questions.rationale: Alarm-safety programs should reduce unnecessary/nonactionable alarm burden without suppressing clinically important alarms. Settings should be clinically appropriate, actionable alarms must remain detectable, and staff response processes must prevent desensitization and delayed recognition of true emergencies.
questions.source_name: FDA — Human Factors Considerations for Medical Devices and Alarm Safety
questions.source_detail: FDA human-factors guidance recognizes that alarm noise and poorly designed alarm management can impair detection and response to clinically important signals.

questions.stem: A client on Contact Precautions for a multidrug-resistant organism is discharged. Before a high-risk client is admitted to the same room, what environmental action is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Change the bed linens and leave reusable equipment in the room because standard detergent cleaning is sufficient once the colonized client has departed.","B":"Clean visibly soiled surfaces and high-touch areas, but leave low-touch surfaces for scheduled cleaning because the patient has already left the room.","C":"Move shared equipment directly to the next room after wiping handles with water because terminal cleaning applies to the room but not to noncritical equipment.","D":"Perform terminal cleaning and disinfection of the room and reprocess reusable equipment according to facility procedures before admitting the next client."}}
questions.rationale: CDC terminal/discharge cleaning includes cleaning and disinfection of high- and low-touch surfaces and reprocessing reusable noncritical patient-care equipment before the next patient occupies the space. Linen change or visible-surface cleaning alone is insufficient.
questions.source_name: CDC — Environmental Cleaning Procedures
questions.source_detail: CDC terminal cleaning after discharge/transfer includes cleaning and disinfecting the patient-care area and reprocessing reusable noncritical equipment.

questions.stem: A nurse assigned to care for patients requiring N95 respiratory protection was last fit-tested 14 months ago and has had no facial changes. What is required before continued use?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Complete another fit test because a tight-fitting respirator requires fit testing before initial use, after a facepiece change, and at least annually thereafter.","B":"Continue with the existing fit test because annual retesting is unnecessary when the same respirator model and size are used and facial features have not changed.","C":"Replace fit testing with a user seal check because a successful seal check at each use satisfies the OSHA requirement for periodic respirator fit testing.","D":"Repeat the medical evaluation instead of fit testing because periodic medical clearance is the requirement that determines continued respirator use."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA requires fit testing for tight-fitting respirators before initial use, whenever a different facepiece is used, and at least annually thereafter. Additional fit testing is required when physical changes could affect fit; a user seal check does not replace required fit testing.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Respiratory Protection Standard
questions.source_detail: 29 CFR 1910.134(f): fit testing before initial use, when a different facepiece is used, and at least annually thereafter; additional testing for physical changes affecting fit.

questions.stem: During a mass-casualty incident using the START adult triage algorithm, an adult victim remains apneic after the airway is repositioned. How is this victim categorized in START?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Red/immediate, because any victim with an airway problem receives the highest transport priority even when breathing does not resume after airway repositioning.","B":"Black/expectant under the START algorithm, because absence of spontaneous breathing after airway repositioning does not meet criteria for the immediate category.","C":"Yellow/delayed, because the absence of breathing indicates severe injury but allows transport to be postponed while victims with circulation problems are treated first.","D":"Green/minor, because respiratory categorization occurs after ambulatory victims have been separated and the victim can be reassessed during transport."}}
questions.rationale: In the START adult triage algorithm, an apneic victim whose breathing does not resume after airway repositioning is categorized black/expectant. The algorithm is a disaster-triage allocation tool and differs from routine single-patient resuscitation.
questions.source_name: HHS REMM — START Adult Triage Algorithm
questions.source_detail: START adult triage uses respiratory status first; no spontaneous breathing after airway repositioning leads to the black/expectant category.

questions.stem: A nurse accidentally emails unsecured PHI to the wrong recipient, who confirms opening and reading it. What should the nurse do next?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Delete the sent message from the nurse's mailbox and take no further action because removing the local copy eliminates the privacy risk created by the disclosure.","B":"Send an individual breach notice and report directly to HHS before the privacy office evaluates whether an exception or low-probability-of-compromise determination applies.","C":"Ask the recipient to keep the information confidential and close the incident because voluntary cooperation removes the disclosure from HIPAA breach requirements.","D":"Report the incident promptly through the organization's privacy process so mitigation, breach-risk assessment, and required notifications can be completed safely."}}
questions.rationale: An impermissible disclosure of unsecured PHI is presumed to be a breach unless the covered entity demonstrates a low probability of compromise using the required risk assessment. The workforce member should promptly report the incident through the organization's privacy process so mitigation, risk assessment, and any required individual/HHS notifications can occur.
questions.source_name: HHS — HIPAA Breach Notification Rule
questions.source_detail: Impermissible unsecured-PHI disclosures require breach risk assessment and, when applicable, notification; current HHS guidance also specifies reporting obligations and timelines.

questions.stem: A client with an unpaid hospital balance requests a copy of the designated medical record set. Which response is most accurate under HIPAA?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The hospital may deny access until the balance is paid because financial obligations take priority over the patient's access rights to protected health information.","B":"The entity may postpone access until the outstanding balance is resolved because account status can be addressed before the HIPAA access deadline begins.","C":"With limited exceptions, the client has a right to access these records and the request must be handled within HIPAA timelines despite the unpaid account balance.","D":"The client may inspect the designated record set but is not entitled to receive a copy unless a clinician determines that providing one is medically necessary."}}
questions.rationale: HIPAA gives individuals a broad right of access to protected health information in a designated record set, subject to limited exceptions. A covered entity may not condition this access right on payment of an unrelated medical bill, and requests must be handled within applicable HIPAA timelines.
questions.source_name: HHS — Individuals' Right of Access under HIPAA
questions.source_detail: HIPAA provides a broad right to inspect or obtain copies of PHI in a designated record set, subject to limited exceptions and response-time requirements.

questions.stem: A competent client says that cultural and religious beliefs make family participation important in end-of-life decisions. What is the nurse's best approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ask the client how family members should be involved, clarify the client's preferences, and incorporate those preferences into care when clinically and legally feasible.","B":"Assume the family should make decisions because clients from cultures that value collective decision-making generally prefer to transfer personal authority to relatives.","C":"Exclude the family from discussions because patient autonomy requires individual decision-making and does not permit culturally preferred family participation.","D":"Ask the oldest family member to decide how information should be shared because age-based hierarchy is the safest way to avoid stereotyping the client's preferences."}}
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive care centers the competent client's stated values and preferences rather than stereotypes. The nurse should ask how the client wants family involved and incorporate those preferences when clinically and legally feasible; the patient retains the right to participate in care planning and informed decisions.
questions.source_name: HHS National CLAS Standards + eCFR Patient Rights
questions.source_detail: HHS National CLAS Standards, Principal Standard 1: respectful care responsive to cultural health beliefs/practices and communication needs; Think Cultural Health current standards page reviewed 2026-08-15. Cross-check: 42 CFR §482.13(b)(1)-(2) gives the patient the right to participate in the plan of care and make informed decisions; current eCFR reviewed 2026-08-15 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-482/subpart-B/section-482.13).

questions.stem: A client with limited English proficiency needs informed consent for a nonemergent procedure. The client's 15-year-old child offers to interpret. What is the best nursing action?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the child if both client and child agree because family preference removes the need for qualified language assistance during a high-stakes consent discussion.","B":"Have the client sign the English form first, then obtain interpretation afterward because the signature documents consent even if comprehension is established later.","C":"Ask any bilingual employee nearby to interpret because conversational fluency is sufficient for complex medical consent even without interpreter qualification.","D":"Arrange qualified language assistance and avoid using the minor child for this nonemergent consent discussion so the client can understand and participate fully."}}
questions.rationale: HHS CLAS standards call for competent language assistance and specifically advise avoiding untrained individuals and minors as interpreters. For nonemergent informed consent, qualified language assistance supports meaningful understanding and participation.
questions.source_name: HHS Office of Minority Health — National CLAS Standards
questions.source_detail: Language assistance should be competent and provided without charge; use of untrained individuals and minors as interpreters should be avoided and discouraged.

questions.stem: A Medicare beneficiary with a terminal illness is considering the hospice benefit and asks whether hospice means all medical treatment stops. Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The hospice election ends Medicare coverage for treatment of both the terminal illness and unrelated conditions because the hospice assumes responsibility for the client's care.","B":"Hospice shifts care for the terminal illness toward comfort and symptom management; Medicare generally stops paying for curative treatment of that terminal illness.","C":"Hospice permits Medicare payment for ongoing curative treatment of the terminal illness when the hospice team also provides a separate comfort-focused plan.","D":"Hospice eligibility means disease-directed treatment must be stopped for coexisting conditions as well as the terminal illness before comfort services can begin."}}
questions.rationale: Hospice changes the focus for the terminal illness to comfort and palliative symptom management rather than cure. Under the Medicare hospice election, the beneficiary waives Medicare payment for curative treatment of the terminal illness and related conditions; this does not mean all care for unrelated conditions stops.
questions.source_name: CMS — Hospice Coverage
questions.source_detail: CMS describes hospice as holistic terminal-illness care focused on comfort/palliative symptom management rather than cure and explains the Medicare hospice election.

questions.stem: A nurse holds an active multistate license under the Nurse Licensure Compact and plans to work temporarily in another NLC jurisdiction. Which statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The multistate license permits practice in compact and noncompact jurisdictions as long as the nurse's primary state of residence remains an NLC member.","B":"The nurse follows the home state's scope-of-practice rules while using the multistate privilege because the license itself was issued by the home-state board.","C":"The license allows practice in other NLC jurisdictions without separate licenses, while the nurse remains subject to the practice laws of the state where care occurs.","D":"The multistate privilege covers in-person nursing in other NLC jurisdictions, while telehealth still requires a separate single-state license in the patient's location."}}
questions.rationale: A multistate license allows nursing practice in other NLC jurisdictions without separate licenses while compact eligibility is maintained. Practice remains subject to the laws and rules of the jurisdiction where the patient is located and nursing practice occurs.
questions.source_name: Nurse Licensure Compact — Nurses & the NLC
questions.source_detail: A multistate license permits practice in other NLC states/territories without additional licenses; telehealth is included and nurses practice under the applicable remote-state authority.

questions.stem: A nurse licensed in State A conducts telehealth with a client who is physically located in State B during the visit. Which licensure principle applies?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Practice occurs where the patient is located, so the nurse needs authority in State B through a license, compact privilege, or another applicable exception as needed.","B":"The nurse's physical location controls licensure for telehealth, so State A authority is sufficient when the nurse remains in State A throughout the encounter.","C":"The client's location becomes a licensure issue when the encounter includes prescribing, while assessment and nursing counseling are governed by the nurse's location.","D":"The nurse may choose which state's rules govern the encounter as long as the client consents to telehealth and the nurse documents the choice in the medical record."}}
questions.rationale: NLC guidance states that nurses must be licensed or otherwise authorized in the state where the patient is located when nursing service is provided. A multistate license can supply that authority when the patient is in another NLC jurisdiction.
questions.source_name: Nurse Licensure Compact — Telehealth and the NLC
questions.source_detail: NLC guidance states that a nurse must be licensed in the state where the patient/consumer is located at the time nursing service is provided, including telehealth.

questions.stem: A client has crushing chest pain and an ECG showing new ST-segment elevation that meets current STEMI diagnostic criteria in anatomically contiguous leads. Troponin results are still pending. What is the priority interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait for a positive troponin before activating the reperfusion pathway because ST-segment elevation alone cannot justify time-sensitive STEMI management.","B":"Treat the tracing as stable angina until serial biomarkers are completed because myocardial infarction cannot be classified during the first hours of symptoms.","C":"Repeat the ECG after several hours and defer escalation if pain improves because transient symptom relief reliably excludes an acute coronary occlusion syndrome.","D":"Activate the time-sensitive STEMI reperfusion pathway based on the clinical presentation and ECG findings rather than waiting for troponin confirmation alone."}}
questions.rationale: The 2025 multisociety acute coronary syndromes guideline treats ECG-confirmed STEMI as a time-sensitive reperfusion emergency. When the clinical presentation and ECG meet STEMI criteria, reperfusion management should not be delayed solely to await cardiac biomarker confirmation.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI — 2025 Acute Coronary Syndromes Guideline
questions.source_detail: 2025 multisociety ACS guideline, JACC, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009: in ECG-confirmed STEMI, reperfusion management is time-sensitive and should not be delayed solely for biomarker confirmation. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client has progressive dyspnea, peripheral edema, and jugular venous distention. The provider orders BNP. How should the nurse understand this test?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An elevated BNP confirms heart failure by itself and removes the need to consider renal function, age, rhythm disorders, imaging findings, or the rest of the clinical picture.","B":"BNP is a useful biomarker that can support the diagnosis and assessment of heart failure, but the value should be interpreted with symptoms, examination, and other testing.","C":"BNP is primarily a marker of pancreatic inflammation, so elevation in a client with dyspnea points away from a cardiovascular cause of the current symptoms.","D":"BNP is mainly useful for prognosis after heart failure is established, so it should not be used to support the diagnostic evaluation of a new dyspnea presentation."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure states that elevated BNP or NT-proBNP can increase diagnostic certainty, but heart failure is established by an accumulation of symptoms, signs, and laboratory or imaging evidence rather than by a single test. BNP therefore supports, but does not independently establish, the diagnosis.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF — Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure (2026)
questions.source_detail: 2026 AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF Expert Consensus Document, definition of HF syndrome: diagnostic certainty is amplified by elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, while HF is defined by an accumulation of suggestive features in comprehensive assessment rather than a single diagnostic test. Published online 2026-06-29, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2026.05.036; reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client with COPD practices pursed-lip breathing during episodes of dyspnea. What is the main physiologic benefit of this technique?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It shortens exhalation and increases breathing frequency so additional breaths occur before small airways can narrow during expiration.","B":"It increases inspired oxygen concentration by retaining exhaled oxygen near the mouth, which raises the oxygen percentage of the next breath.","C":"It prolongs exhalation and creates back-pressure that keeps small airways open longer, helping trapped air leave the lungs more effectively.","D":"It lowers airway pressure during exhalation so small airways close earlier, limiting how much air can remain trapped after each breath."}}
questions.rationale: Pursed-lip breathing slows and prolongs exhalation, helping keep small airways open longer so trapped air can leave the lungs more effectively. It does not increase the oxygen concentration of room air or intentionally accelerate breathing.
questions.source_name: American Lung Association — Breathing Exercises
questions.source_detail: Pursed-lip breathing slows breathing, keeps airways open longer, and helps remove trapped air from the lungs.

questions.stem: After a generalized tonic-clonic seizure ends, the client remains unresponsive but is breathing spontaneously. What should the nurse do first during postictal recovery?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Turn the client onto the side, maintain a clear airway, assess breathing and injury, and remain nearby until awareness and protective responses begin to return.","B":"Insert a padded object between the teeth before the jaw relaxes because preventing tongue injury takes priority while the client remains unresponsive.","C":"Offer water or oral medication as soon as convulsive movements stop because swallowing usually returns before consciousness during postictal recovery.","D":"Hold the client firmly in a supine position until fully alert because restricting movement reduces aspiration and injury during postictal confusion or agitation."}}
questions.rationale: Current seizure first aid emphasizes Stay, Safe, Side. A person who is not awake should be positioned on the side to help maintain the airway, observed for breathing and injury, and monitored until awake and alert. Objects should not be placed in the mouth, oral intake should wait until the person is fully awake, and restraint should be avoided.
questions.source_name: Epilepsy Foundation — Seizure First Aid: Stay, Safe, Side
questions.source_detail: Current 2026 first-aid guidance: stay with the person, keep them safe, turn an unresponsive person on the side, do not put objects in the mouth, and do not give food/water until awake.

questions.stem: Two weeks after abdominal surgery, a client develops worsening crampy abdominal pain, progressive distention, repeated vomiting, and no passage of stool or flatus. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's priority response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The pattern is most consistent with uncomplicated postoperative constipation, so routine bowel-care measures can continue while the client is observed for another day.","B":"The symptoms are most consistent with transient indigestion after surgery, so oral intake can be advanced as tolerated while discomfort is reassessed.","C":"The findings fit a urinary complication more than a gastrointestinal problem, so the priority is urine testing before the abdominal symptoms are escalated.","D":"The combination raises concern for postoperative small-bowel obstruction and warrants prompt surgical evaluation rather than routine constipation treatment."}}
questions.rationale: Prior abdominal surgery is a major risk factor for adhesive small-bowel obstruction. The combination of crampy abdominal pain, progressive distention, repeated vomiting, and obstipation two weeks after surgery warrants prompt evaluation for postoperative small-bowel obstruction rather than routine constipation treatment. Moving the scenario beyond the immediate postoperative period removes the prior ileus-versus-obstruction ambiguity.
questions.source_name: World Society of Emergency Surgery — Bologna Guidelines for Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction
questions.source_detail: WSES Bologna evidence-based guideline, DOI 10.1186/s13017-018-0185-2: prior abdominal surgery is a major cause of adhesive SBO; abdominal pain, vomiting, distention and constipation/obstipation are characteristic. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and overt hepatic encephalopathy is receiving lactulose. Which explanation best describes why the nurse titrates therapy to regular soft bowel movements?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lactulose acidifies the colon, traps ammonia as ammonium, and promotes fecal elimination of nitrogenous compounds that contribute to hepatic encephalopathy.","B":"Lactulose restores damaged hepatocytes directly, allowing the liver to resume normal ammonia metabolism before neurologic symptoms can recur during treatment.","C":"Lactulose increases intestinal protein absorption so fewer amino acids reach the colon for bacterial metabolism during recurrent episodes of encephalopathy.","D":"Lactulose suppresses renal ammonium excretion and shifts nitrogen elimination toward the kidneys, lowering ammonia mainly through enhanced urinary clearance."}}
questions.rationale: Lactulose reaches the colon largely unchanged, where bacterial metabolism acidifies the colonic contents. This favors conversion of ammonia to ammonium, reducing absorption and promoting fecal elimination. The drug is used for prevention and treatment of portal-systemic encephalopathy; it does not repair hepatocytes or work mainly through renal nitrogen clearance.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Lactulose Solution, USP
questions.source_detail: 2026 lactulose labeling describes colonic acidification, trapping of ammonia as ammonium, and laxative elimination in portal-systemic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has glucose 820 mg/dL, marked dehydration, effective serum osmolality 326 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, and no severe ketonemia. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Diabetic ketoacidosis, because severe hyperglycemia by itself establishes DKA even when clinically important ketonemia and metabolic acidosis are absent.","B":"Stress hyperglycemia, because dehydration and altered osmolality exclude a hyperglycemic crisis when the bicarbonate concentration remains above 18 mmol/L.","C":"Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, because marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality occur without the severe ketonemia and metabolic acidosis required for DKA.","D":"Euglycemic ketoacidosis, because the relatively preserved pH is more important than the markedly elevated glucose and hyperosmolar state in classifying the crisis."}}
questions.rationale: The current ADA-led consensus defines HHS by significant hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without severe ketonemia or metabolic acidosis. DKA requires diabetes/hyperglycemia together with elevated ketones and metabolic acidosis. Mixed presentations can occur, but the data in this item fit HHS.
questions.source_name: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
questions.source_detail: 2024 consensus diagnostic framework: HHS requires hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality in the absence of severe ketonemia and metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A client with an acute cervical spinal cord injury becomes hypotensive with a heart rate of 48/min and warm, dry skin. No major external bleeding is identified. Which shock state should the nurse suspect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypovolemic shock, because loss of circulating volume typically produces hypotension with relative bradycardia and warm peripheral vasodilation after trauma.","B":"Neurogenic shock, because disruption of sympathetic outflow after high spinal injury can produce vasodilation, hypotension, and inappropriate bradycardia.","C":"Cardiogenic shock, because pump failure after trauma commonly produces warm skin and bradycardia without pulmonary congestion or another cardiac finding.","D":"Obstructive shock, because impaired venous return from tension physiology typically produces bradycardia and warm extremities before respiratory findings develop."}}
questions.rationale: High spinal cord injury can interrupt sympathetic tone, causing peripheral vasodilation and hypotension with bradycardia rather than the compensatory tachycardia expected in most other shock states. The warm, dry skin and absence of major blood loss support neurogenic shock in this scenario.
questions.source_name: American College of Surgeons / Trauma Care — Neurogenic Shock After Spinal Cord Injury
questions.source_detail: Neurogenic shock after high spinal cord injury is characterized by loss of sympathetic tone, vasodilation, hypotension, and often bradycardia.

questions.stem: A client with epigastric pain radiating to the back recently had parotitis, and the provider is evaluating possible acute pancreatitis. Which laboratory result would be more useful than amylase for supporting pancreatic injury in this setting?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A serum sodium concentration above the reference range, because sodium is more pancreas-specific than digestive enzymes when salivary disease is also present.","B":"A serum potassium concentration below the reference range, because potassium falls specifically with pancreatic inflammation but not with salivary-gland disease.","C":"A serum lipase concentration markedly above the upper reference limit, because lipase is more specific for pancreatic injury than amylase in this clinical context.","D":"A repeat serum amylase concentration alone, because amylase remains pancreas-specific even when a recent salivary-gland disorder can also elevate that enzyme level."}}
questions.rationale: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from compatible pain, characteristic imaging, and/or pancreatic enzyme elevation. Lipase is preferred clinically because it is more specific for pancreatic injury than amylase, which can rise with salivary-gland disease and other nonpancreatic conditions.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Clinical Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis
questions.source_detail: ACG guidance uses compatible symptoms, imaging, and pancreatic enzymes in diagnosis; lipase is preferred over amylase when nonpancreatic amylase elevation is a concern.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with systemic inflammation, edema, poor intake, and a serum albumin of 2.5 g/dL is referred for nutrition assessment. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The albumin value confirms protein-calorie malnutrition by itself and can be used as the primary marker to quantify the severity of the client's nutrition deficit.","B":"The albumin value primarily measures recent protein intake, so normalization after several meals would reliably demonstrate that the client's nutrition deficit has resolved.","C":"The albumin value is unaffected by inflammation or capillary permeability, making it a specific marker of total body protein in acutely ill hospitalized clients.","D":"The low albumin is associated with inflammation and adverse-outcome risk but cannot diagnose malnutrition by itself; nutrition assessment must use clinical and intake data."}}
questions.rationale: ASPEN specifically advises that serum albumin and prealbumin should not be used as nutrition markers or proxy measures of total body protein. Their concentrations fall with inflammation and altered capillary permeability and are better interpreted as markers associated with illness severity and nutrition risk. Diagnosis of malnutrition requires broader clinical assessment.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — The Use of Visceral Proteins as Nutrition Markers: Position Paper
questions.source_detail: ASPEN states that albumin and prealbumin characterize inflammation rather than nutrition status and should not be used to diagnose protein-energy malnutrition.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis becomes newly confused and has asterixis. The serum ammonia level is elevated. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's clinical reasoning?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The presentation is compatible with hepatic encephalopathy, but the diagnosis and severity are clinical; the ammonia value alone should not be used to grade or confirm the syndrome.","B":"The elevated ammonia concentration confirms both the diagnosis and the exact grade of hepatic encephalopathy, so no further assessment for other causes of confusion is needed.","C":"The ammonia result rules out hepatic encephalopathy because clinically important encephalopathy generally occurs only when ammonia values remain within the reference range.","D":"The serum ammonia value should determine the lactulose dose independently of neurologic findings, bowel response, precipitating factors, and the client's overall clinical course over time."}}
questions.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis. AASLD notes that ammonia levels do not consistently correlate with the presence or severity of encephalopathy and should not be used alone to rule in or grade HE. Other causes and precipitating factors for altered mental status still require assessment.
questions.source_name: AASLD — Ammonia and Hepatic Encephalopathy
questions.source_detail: AASLD: ammonia levels do not consistently correlate with HE severity; HE remains a clinical diagnosis and alternative causes/precipitants should be evaluated.

questions.stem: A client reports fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated TSH. Which additional result would most strongly support primary hypothyroidism?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An elevated free T4 concentration, because primary hypothyroidism is characterized by increased pituitary TSH and increased circulating thyroid hormone.","B":"A low free T4 concentration, because elevated TSH together with reduced circulating free T4 is the classic biochemical pattern of primary hypothyroidism.","C":"A suppressed TSH on repeat testing, because primary hypothyroidism ordinarily causes simultaneous suppression of both TSH and circulating free thyroid hormone.","D":"An isolated elevated total T3 concentration, because T3 is the most reliable confirmatory test for primary hypothyroidism when the TSH is markedly increased."}}
questions.rationale: The American Thyroid Association describes elevated TSH with low free T4 (or free T4 index) as the typical biochemical pattern of primary hypothyroidism. T3 testing is much more useful in evaluating hyperthyroidism and may remain normal even in significant hypothyroidism.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Thyroid Function Tests
questions.source_detail: ATA: elevated TSH plus low FT4/FTI indicates primary hypothyroidism; T3 is not the preferred confirmatory test for hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A client with recurrent gout is taking urate-lowering therapy. Which laboratory goal best reflects the treat-to-target approach recommended for long-term gout management?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Maintain serum urate above the saturation range so existing crystals remain stable and additional inflammatory flares are less likely to occur.","B":"Use symptoms alone and avoid serial serum urate measurements because laboratory targets have no role once urate-lowering therapy has been started.","C":"Titrate urate-lowering therapy toward a serum urate target below 6 mg/dL while monitoring adherence, tolerability, and the client's clinical course.","D":"Stop urate-lowering therapy as soon as the first flare-free month occurs, because continuing treatment below a serum urate target increases crystal formation."}}
questions.rationale: The American College of Rheumatology gout guideline strongly supports a treat-to-target strategy for patients receiving urate-lowering therapy, with dose titration guided by serial serum urate and a target below 6 mg/dL. Urate-lowering therapy is long-term disease management, not something stopped after a brief flare-free period.
questions.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — 2020 Guideline for the Management of Gout
questions.source_detail: ACR recommends treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy with serial serum urate measurements and a target serum urate below 6 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has an elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin but no ischemic symptoms or new ECG changes. Which statement best reflects how the nurse should interpret this result?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Any troponin value above the reference limit establishes an acute myocardial infarction regardless of symptoms, ECG findings, serial change, or the clinical context.","B":"Troponin elevation identifies skeletal-muscle injury rather than myocardial injury, so the result has little relevance when the client has chronic kidney disease.","C":"A single elevated troponin rules out acute coronary syndrome because myocardial infarction requires troponin values to remain within the reference interval.","D":"Troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury, but myocardial infarction requires clinical evidence of acute ischemia and interpretation of the pattern in context."}}
questions.rationale: Cardiac troponin above the 99th-percentile reference limit establishes myocardial injury, not automatically myocardial infarction. The universal definition of MI requires integration of a rise/fall pattern when appropriate with evidence of acute ischemia such as ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, imaging, or coronary thrombus. Chronic kidney disease is one setting in which troponin may be chronically elevated.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF — Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction
questions.source_detail: Troponin elevation means myocardial injury; diagnosis of MI requires clinical evidence of acute ischemia and integrated biomarker/ECG/clinical assessment.

questions.stem: An immobile hospitalized client is at high risk for pressure injury and is lying on a pressure-redistributing support surface. Which repositioning plan is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Individualize the turning frequency based on the support surface, skin response, mobility, perfusion, tolerance, and other risk factors, while continuing regular repositioning.","B":"Use a fixed two-hour schedule for every at-risk client because support surface, tissue tolerance, sleep, perfusion, body size, and individual risk do not alter repositioning needs.","C":"Stop routine repositioning once a pressure-redistributing mattress is in place because the support surface removes clinically meaningful pressure-injury risk.","D":"Reposition only after nonblanchable erythema appears because turning before visible skin injury has not been shown to contribute to pressure-injury prevention."}}
questions.rationale: Current pressure-injury prevention guidance supports regular repositioning but does not require one universal interval for every patient. Frequency should be individualized according to the support surface, tissue tolerance, mobility, perfusion, clinical condition, and patient preferences. A support surface does not eliminate the need to reposition.
questions.source_name: National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel — Pressure Injury Prevention / International Guideline
questions.source_detail: NPIAP guidance supports individualized repositioning frequency based on support surface, skin/tissue tolerance, mobility and other patient-specific risk factors.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old adult has dry mouth and delayed skin recoil. A colleague says these findings alone confirm low-intake dehydration. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use delayed skin recoil as sufficient evidence of low-intake dehydration because age-related changes do not materially reduce the specificity of this sign.","B":"Do not diagnose low-intake dehydration from simple bedside signs alone; in an older adult, use a broader assessment and measured serum or plasma osmolality.","C":"Use urine color as the preferred confirmatory test because it remains a reliable stand-alone marker of low-intake dehydration in older adults.","D":"Exclude dehydration when the oral mucosa is moist because one normal bedside finding is enough to rule out a clinically important water deficit in an older adult."}}
questions.rationale: ESPEN recommends directly measured serum or plasma osmolality when evaluating low-intake dehydration in older adults and specifically advises against diagnosing it from simple signs such as skin turgor, mouth dryness, urine color, or similar bedside findings alone. The prior item conflated low-intake dehydration with volume depletion and therefore required a substantive rewrite.
questions.source_name: ESPEN — Practical Guideline: Clinical Nutrition and Hydration in Geriatrics
questions.source_detail: ESPEN Practical Guideline, recommendations 65 and 68: use directly measured serum/plasma osmolality to evaluate low-intake dehydration; simple bedside signs including skin turgor and mouth dryness should not be used alone to diagnose it in older adults. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client has right-leg weakness after hip surgery and is beginning cane training. Which technique provides the best mechanical support during level ambulation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hold the cane in the right hand and advance it after the stronger left leg so the cane remains on the same side as the weaker extremity during each step of gait.","B":"Alternate the cane between hands every few steps so both upper extremities share the load equally and the client avoids developing a side preference.","C":"Hold the cane in the left hand and advance the cane with the weaker right leg, allowing the device to widen the base of support and unload the affected side.","D":"Place the cane directly in front of both feet and advance both legs together toward it so the device functions as a single central point of balance."}}
questions.rationale: A cane is generally held contralateral to the weaker or painful lower extremity. Advancing the cane with the affected leg helps widen the base of support and reduces load through the involved side. Device choice and gait pattern should still follow the client's postoperative precautions and rehabilitation plan.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Assistive Devices and Gait Training
questions.source_detail: Standard cane gait uses the cane on the stronger/opposite side and advances it with the weaker affected leg unless a patient-specific rehabilitation plan directs otherwise.

questions.stem: A client receiving intermittent gastric tube feedings had nausea and abdominal distention during the previous feeding. Which assessment approach is most appropriate before the next feeding?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the pump's programmed rate as the sole indicator of tolerance because subjective symptoms, abdominal findings, and stool or flatus patterns do not reliably affect feeding decisions.","B":"Automatically stop all enteral nutrition whenever any measurable gastric residual is obtained, even when the client has no other evidence of feeding intolerance.","C":"Rely only on the presence of bowel sounds because bowel sounds are the most accurate single measure of aspiration risk and gastric emptying in enterally fed clients.","D":"Assess the client's symptoms and abdominal findings and follow the facility's evidence-based protocol; do not rely on a single gastric residual value as the sole tolerance measure."}}
questions.rationale: ASPEN recommends evaluating enteral-feeding tolerance using multiple clinical parameters such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention, pain, stool/flatus patterns, physical findings, and the overall clinical course. Gastric residual volume should not be used as a stand-alone determinant of tolerance, and routine GRV monitoring may not be necessary in some settings.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Safe Practices for Enteral Nutrition Therapy
questions.source_detail: ASPEN recommends a multidimensional assessment of enteral-feeding tolerance and cautions against relying solely on gastric residual volume.

questions.stem: An adult client wants a realistic weekly physical-activity goal for general health. Which plan best matches current U.S. public-health guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week and include muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days during the week.","B":"Limit activity to one short session each week because additional moderate aerobic activity provides no measurable health benefit in otherwise healthy adults.","C":"Complete at least 10 hours of vigorous exercise every week before adding any muscle-strengthening activity, regardless of baseline fitness or medical history.","D":"Avoid structured physical activity unless weight loss is the primary goal because aerobic and resistance exercise are not recommended for general health maintenance."}}
questions.rationale: CDC guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or an equivalent amount of vigorous/mixed activity, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days each week. Some activity is better than none, and goals can be adapted to the person's condition and abilities.
questions.source_name: CDC — Adult Physical Activity Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Current CDC guidance: adults need at least 150 minutes/week moderate-intensity aerobic activity plus muscle strengthening on 2 or more days.

questions.stem: A parent asks when a healthy toddler should be switched from a rear-facing car safety seat to a forward-facing seat. Which teaching is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Switch the child at the second birthday regardless of size because age alone determines when rear-facing protection should end for every toddler.","B":"Keep the child rear-facing as long as possible until the child reaches the rear-facing height or weight limit specified by the seat manufacturer.","C":"Turn the child forward-facing once independent walking begins because motor development is a more important criterion than the restraint system's size limits.","D":"Move directly to a belt-positioning booster when the child becomes uncomfortable rear-facing even if the forward-facing harness limits have not been reached."}}
questions.rationale: The AAP recommends that infants and toddlers remain rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the highest rear-facing weight or height allowed by the car-seat manufacturer. The policy was reaffirmed in 2025. Transition decisions are therefore based on the restraint system's limits rather than a fixed second birthday.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Child Passenger Safety
questions.source_detail: AAP policy, reaffirmed 2025: infants and toddlers should remain rear-facing until they exceed the manufacturer's rear-facing height or weight limit.

questions.stem: During a preventive visit, an adult completes the three-item AUDIT-C alcohol screen and has a positive result. What should the nurse understand about this finding?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The result establishes alcoholic liver disease and eliminates the need to ask further questions about quantity, frequency, impairment, or other health consequences.","B":"The result directly diagnoses alcohol use disorder and should be treated as equivalent to a complete diagnostic assessment using current DSM-based clinical criteria.","C":"The result identifies possible unhealthy alcohol use and should prompt further assessment and, when appropriate, brief intervention rather than serve as a diagnosis.","D":"The result estimates the client's current blood alcohol concentration and is useful primarily for determining whether the client is legally intoxicated at the visit."}}
questions.rationale: AUDIT-C is a validated brief screening tool for unhealthy alcohol use. A positive result indicates the need for further assessment; it does not by itself diagnose alcohol use disorder, liver disease, or current intoxication. Subsequent clinical assessment determines the appropriate brief intervention, treatment evaluation, or referral.
questions.source_name: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism — Alcohol Screening and AUDIT-C
questions.source_detail: NIAAA identifies AUDIT-C as a recommended brief adult alcohol screening tool; positive screening requires further clinical assessment rather than constituting a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client suddenly becomes intensely anxious, is pacing, breathing rapidly, and says, 'Something terrible is happening.' Initial vital signs are being obtained. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin a detailed exploration of recent and remote psychological stressors immediately because identifying the source is more urgent than reducing stimulation or completing safety assessment.","B":"Leave the client alone in a quiet room because staff presence may reinforce anxiety and interfere with the client's ability to regain control without additional support.","C":"Assume the symptoms are psychiatric once anxiety is visible and postpone assessment for medical causes such as hypoxemia, arrhythmia, medication effects, or metabolic disturbance.","D":"Remain with the client, use calm brief communication, reduce stimulation, and continue assessment for immediate safety and possible medical contributors while helping the client settle."}}
questions.rationale: Severe anxiety can impair the ability to process complex information. Nursing care should provide safety, calm presence, concise communication, and reduced stimulation while also assessing for medical causes of acute autonomic symptoms rather than assuming the presentation is purely psychiatric. Detailed exploration is deferred until the client can engage effectively.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing: Mental Health and Community Concepts, Anxiety Management
questions.source_detail: Acute severe anxiety management prioritizes safety, calm simple communication, decreased stimulation, and assessment for possible medical contributors before detailed exploration.

questions.stem: A client becomes increasingly agitated after learning that a family visit is delayed. The client is shouting but has not threatened anyone or attempted violence. Which staff approach best supports verbal de-escalation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use one calm speaker, maintain nonthreatening body language and appropriate personal space, acknowledge the concern, set clear limits, and offer realistic choices when possible.","B":"Have several staff members speak at the same time from close range so the client clearly understands that the team has control of the situation and expects immediate compliance.","C":"Match the client's volume and intensity to demonstrate authority, then challenge inaccurate statements point by point until the client admits the behavior is inappropriate.","D":"Move directly to physical restraint because raised voice alone predicts imminent violence and verbal strategies should not be attempted once visible agitation has begun."}}
questions.rationale: Effective de-escalation emphasizes a calm, nonconfrontational approach, respect for personal space, clear communication, active listening, limit setting, and offering reasonable choices when safety permits. Restrictive interventions are not justified solely by raised voice and should not replace less-restrictive approaches when those remain feasible.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — De-escalation in Health Care / Workplace Violence Prevention
questions.source_detail: De-escalation uses calm nonconfrontational communication, personal-space awareness, clear limits, active listening and least-restrictive strategies before escalation when safely feasible.
